builder_plan.scenario: Your workload might fit a smaller or differently structured model.
builder_plan.change: Check for available weights and a compatible runtime before planning a product trial.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current model on identical held-out tasks and the same resource budget.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Task success, latency, memory, context limits, and migration cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Library of Layers (LoL): Adaptively Ordering Transformer Layers at Runtime
summary: LoL replaces the fixed sequential execution of transformer layers with a router that dynamically orders a shared library of blocks at inference, unifying dense, depth-recurrent, and MoE-style compute allocation in one architecture. It costs a full custom pretraining run (infeasible on a single 24 GB GPU or API budget), added router complexity at inference, and it cannot be retrofitted onto existing pretrained checkpoints or accessed through third-party APIs. Routing can be unstable or uninterpretable in practice, gains over baselines are stated as merely competitive rather than superior, and the claimed controllability benefits rest on synthetic tasks that may not transfer to production workloads.
rationale: The method requires training a bespoke architecture from scratch, which is outside the reader's constrained infrastructure, and its performance claims are only parity with baselines, so it warrants monitoring rather than adoption.

claims.statement: LoL replaces the fixed sequential execution of transformer layers with a router that dynamically orders a shared library of blocks at inference, unifying dense, depth-recurrent, and MoE-style compute allocation in one architecture. It costs a full custom pretraining run (infeasible on a single 24 GB GPU or API budget), added router complexity at inference, and it cannot be retrofitted onto existing pretrained checkpoints or accessed through third-party APIs. Routing can be unstable or uninterpretable in practice, gains over baselines are stated as merely competitive rather than superior, and the claimed controllability benefits rest on synthetic tasks that may not transfer to production workloads.

Achieves competitive performance with dense, depth-recurrent, and mixture-of-experts baselines in pretraining, with interpretable layer orderings on synthetic and multilingual tasks; no quantified speedup or efficiency factor is reported.
